Diab1, Wen-tau Yih3, Xin Luna Dong2   1Carnegie Mellon University, 2Meta Reality Labs, 3FAIR at Meta, 4University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, 5University of Toronto, 6Princeton University, 7The University of Tokyo, 8RIKEN AIP ∗Work done during an internship at Meta   Despite rapid progress in automating scientific research, generating promising and well grounded research solutions remains a central challenge. We isolate research ideation as a standalone task and build our solution on the intuition that a challenge in one field can often be addressed by a mechanism that solved an analogous challenge in another. Accordingly, we introduce IdeaScientist, which decomposes ideation into gap finding, innovation, and report writing, and trains each role with reinforcement learning.

To make long-horizon research ideation trainable, we use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024b) to train each subagent role with a stage-matched human reference artifact and rubric, then recompose the trained roles within the full agentic loop.   3 IdeaScientist: A Framework for Autoresearch Ideation   3.1 Harness Design   IdeaScientist decomposes research ideation into three specialized sub-agents coordinated by an orchestrator: a gap finder examines closely related works to identify methodological limitations, an innovator draws on work from different problem settings to develop transferable solution intuitions, and a report writer consolidates the surviving intuition into a complete proposal. The report writer follows a fixed output schema that requires it to formalize the problem setting, state the central novelty, distinguish the proposed mechanism from the closest prior methods, and provide sufficient architectural and training detail to make the proposal actionable. It also specifies an evaluation plan, falsifiable predictions and their refutation conditions, and the proposal’s limitations, while supporting claims about prior work with inline database identifiers. Table 5 provides the complete schema.   The orchestrator maintains the evolving research plan and determines which sub-agent to invoke next, allowing the system to revisit earlier stages when additional evidence or refinement is needed.

We thus draw insights not from prior work in the same domain, but from work addressing a similar challenge in a different field. For example, web search cuts latency by low-cost retrieval of a candidate set before applying a sophisticated ranker; the same two-stage structure answers the latency challenge in recommendation, where first-stage filtering precedes fine-grained scoring.   We introduce IdeaScientist, an agent framework that operationalizes this process with three specialized sub-agents. A gap finder examines closely related prior solutions in the target domain to identify the shared methodological limitation that leaves the challenge unaddressed, or even amplifies it.
